yintang.name: Hall of Impression
yintang.where: On the midline of the forehead, in the hollow exactly between the inner ends of the two eyebrows.
yintang.press: Rest a fingertip there and press lightly (about 3 out of 10) in slow, small circles for 30–60 seconds, with closed eyes and slow breathing.
yintang.use: Traditionally used to calm the mind and for a tight forehead or a stuffy-feeling nose. Many people simply find it relaxing; evidence that it does more is limited.

bl2.name: Bamboo Gathering
bl2.where: In the small notch at the inner end of each eyebrow, on the bone just above the inner corner of the eye.
bl2.press: Press up and slightly in against the brow bone with both thumbs or index fingers, lightly (about 3 out of 10), for 30–60 seconds. Keep off the eye itself.
bl2.use: Traditionally used for tired eyes, screen strain and pressure around the brow. A common step in eye-relaxation routines; evidence is limited.

yuyao.name: Fish Waist
yuyao.where: In the middle of each eyebrow, directly above the pupil when you look straight ahead.
yuyao.press: Press lightly on the eyebrow (about 3 out of 10) with small circles for 30–60 seconds.
yuyao.use: Traditionally used for tired eyes and a tense brow. Evidence is limited.

te23.name: Silk Bamboo Hollow
te23.where: In the small hollow at the outer end of each eyebrow.
te23.press: Light pressure (about 3 out of 10) in small circles for 30–60 seconds.
te23.use: Traditionally used for eye strain and headaches at the side of the head. Evidence is limited.

taiyang.name: Supreme Yang (temple)
taiyang.where: At the temple: find the point halfway between the outer end of the eyebrow and the outer corner of the eye, then move about one finger-width back towards the ear, into the soft hollow.
taiyang.press: Use two or three fingertips and gentle circles (about 3–4 out of 10) for 30–60 seconds. The bone here is thin: never press hard.
taiyang.use: Traditionally used for tension headaches and tired eyes; rubbing the temples is something many people do by instinct. Evidence is limited.

gb1.name: Pupil Bone-Hole
gb1.where: About half a thumb-width (0.5 cun) out from the outer corner of the eye, in the small dip on the edge of the eye socket.
gb1.press: Very light pressure (about 2–3 out of 10) on the bone, not towards the eye, for 30 seconds.
gb1.use: Traditionally used for tired, dry-feeling eyes. Evidence is limited.

st2.name: Four Whites
st2.where: Below the pupil when you look straight ahead, about one finger-width under the lower rim of the eye socket, in a small dip in the cheekbone.
st2.press: Light pressure (about 3 out of 10) on the cheekbone with small circles for 30–60 seconds. Press on bone, never up into the eye.
st2.use: Traditionally used for tired eyes and a blocked-feeling face or sinuses. Evidence is limited.

gb20.name: Wind Pool
gb20.where: At the back of the head, just under the base of the skull, in the hollow on each side between the two big neck muscles, about level with the earlobes.
gb20.press: Hook your thumbs into both hollows and press up towards the skull (4–6 out of 10) for 30–60 seconds, letting the head tilt back slightly. Do not press on the front or sides of the neck.
gb20.use: Traditionally used for tension headaches, a stiff neck and eye strain. Evidence is limited, but pressing the base of the skull is a common way to relax a tight neck.

gb21.name: Shoulder Well
gb21.where: On top of the shoulder, halfway between the bony bump at the base of the neck (C7) and the outer tip of the shoulder, on the highest point of the muscle.
gb21.press: Squeeze or press down into the muscle with the opposite hand's fingers (4–6 out of 10) for 30–60 seconds. Press muscle, not bone.
gb21.use: Traditionally used for tight shoulders and neck tension. Evidence is limited.
gb21.caution: Pregnancy: avoid firm pressure here; traditional practice advises against it.

li4.name: Union Valley
li4.where: On the back of the hand, in the web between the thumb and the index finger: press the thumb against the side of the index finger and it is on the top of the bulge of muscle, about level with the end of the crease. It lies next to the middle of the index finger's long hand bone.
li4.press: Pinch with the thumb of the other hand on top and the index finger underneath, angled towards the index finger's bone, at 4–6 out of 10 for 30–60 seconds. Then swap hands.
li4.use: Traditionally used for headaches, toothache and general tension. It is one of the best known points; a few small studies exist but the evidence is limited.
li4.caution: Pregnancy: avoid firm pressure on this point; traditional practice advises against it.

pc6.name: Inner Pass
pc6.where: On the inside of the forearm, three finger-widths (2 cun) above the main wrist crease, between the two tendons in the middle of the wrist (make a fist and bend the wrist slightly to see them).
pc6.press: Press with the thumb at 4–6 out of 10, steady or in small circles, for 1–2 minutes, then do the other wrist. Travel-sickness bands press this same spot.
pc6.use: Traditionally used for nausea, travel sickness and an unsettled stomach. This is the best-studied point on the map: reviews of trials found that stimulating it may reduce nausea and vomiting after surgery, while results for pregnancy sickness and motion sickness are mixed.

ht7.name: Spirit Gate
ht7.where: On the wrist crease, on the little-finger side, in the small hollow just inside (towards the thumb) the tendon you can feel there.
ht7.press: Press gently with the thumb (about 4 out of 10) for 30–60 seconds while breathing slowly.
ht7.use: Traditionally used to settle the mind before sleep and in times of stress. Evidence is limited.

st36.name: Leg Three Miles
st36.where: Below the knee on the front of the leg: from the dip just below the kneecap on the outer side, go four finger-widths (3 cun) down, then about one finger-width out from the sharp front edge of the shinbone.
st36.press: Press firmly with the thumb or knuckle (5–6 out of 10) in small circles for 1 minute on each leg.
st36.use: Traditionally one of the most used points, for tiredness and digestion. Evidence is limited.

sp6.name: Three Yin Intersection
sp6.where: On the inner side of the lower leg, four finger-widths (3 cun) above the tip of the inner ankle bone, just behind the edge of the shinbone.
sp6.press: Press with the thumb at 4–6 out of 10 for 30–60 seconds. It is often tender.
sp6.use: Traditionally used for period cramps and sleep. A few small trials looked at period pain with mixed results; evidence is limited.
sp6.caution: Pregnancy: avoid firm pressure on this point; traditional practice advises against it.

lr3.name: Great Surge
lr3.where: On the top of the foot, in the hollow between the big toe's and the second toe's long bones: slide a finger up from the web between those toes until it stops where the bones meet.
lr3.press: Press with the thumb at 4–6 out of 10, angled towards the second toe's bone, for 30–60 seconds on each foot.
lr3.use: Traditionally used for stress, irritability and headaches. Evidence is limited.

ki1.name: Gushing Spring
ki1.where: On the sole, in the dip that appears when you curl the toes, just below the ball of the foot, about one third of the way from the base of the second and third toes to the back of the heel.
ki1.press: Press with the thumb or knuckle at 4–6 out of 10 for 30–60 seconds, or roll the sole over a ball. A calm way to end the day.
ki1.use: Traditionally used to feel grounded and calm, for example before sleep. Evidence is limited.

toes.name: Toes
toes.maps: On a reflexology chart the toes stand for the head: the big toe for the brain and the tips for the sinuses.

ball.name: Ball of the foot
ball.maps: The chart maps the ball of the foot to the chest: lungs and upper back, with the heart area on the left foot.

arch.name: Arch
arch.maps: The chart maps the arch to the digestive area: stomach, pancreas and intestines, and the kidneys towards the middle.

heel.name: Heel
heel.maps: The chart maps the heel to the lower back, the hips and the pelvic area.

spine.name: Inner edge
spine.maps: The chart maps the inner edge of the foot, from the big toe to the heel, to the spine: neck at the top, lower back at the bottom.

heart.name: Heart area
heart.maps: In the common chart the heart area is on the ball of the left foot only.

spleen.name: Spleen area
spleen.maps: In the common chart the spleen area is on the outer side of the left foot, just below the ball.

liver.name: Liver and gallbladder area
liver.maps: In the common chart the liver and gallbladder area is on the outer side of the right foot, just below the ball.
